prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current video diffusion models are heavily constrained by fixed training resolutions and aspect ratios, severely limiting their application in immersive environments such as AR/VR which require high-resolution, wide-aspect ratio, or $360^{\circ}$ panoramic content. While techniques exist to stitch static image patches together, extending this to video is non-trivial; simply stitching video patches results in disjointed motion and visible seams. Furthermore, generating high-resolution dynamic scenes globally is computationally prohibitive, often exceeding GPU memory limits. There is a lack of a unified, memory-efficient framework capable of generating spatially scalable and seamless panoramic videos with coherent motion without requiring expensive model retraining.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that a pre-trained, standard video diffusion model can be adapted to generate panoramic and infinite-resolution video *without fine-tuning* by manipulating the denoising process. Our core intuition is that by employing a "shifting window" mechanism—where the field of view processed by the model shifts continuously during the denoising steps—we can distribute semantic and motion coherence across the entire canvas. By creating overlaps across the *diffusion timesteps* rather than just spatial overlaps, we can achieve seamless boundaries and global consistency while maintaining constant memory consumption.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We aim to build a framework named "DynamicScaler" that operates on the latent space of existing video diffusion models. The approach consists of three main strategic components:

**1. Offset Shifting Denoising (OSD)**
Instead of processing the entire high-resolution panorama at once (which causes memory issues) or stitching static windows (which causes seams), we will implement a moving window approach.
*   **Mechanism:** At each denoising timestep, we will divide the large panoramic latent space into smaller windows that fit the base model's input size. Crucially, we will apply an **offset** to these windows both vertically and horizontally between steps.
*   **Intuition:** This ensures that boundary regions in one step become central regions in the next. This "temporal" shifting (across the diffusion process) diffuses consistency across the entire image, eliminating grid-like artifacts and seams. For $360^{\circ}$ content, we will treat the latent space as a cylinder, connecting the left and right boundaries logically to allow windows to wrap around.

**2. Global Motion Guidance (GMG)**
To prevent "motion drift" where different parts of a large panorama move independently (e.g., a waterfall flowing at different speeds in different sectors), we will introduce a hierarchical guidance step.
*   **Process:** We will first generate a low-resolution version of the video to establish the coarse motion structure and layout.
*   **Guidance:** This low-res video will be upscaled and re-noised to serve as a structural prior. During the high-resolution generation (using OSD), this prior will guide the denoising process, ensuring that local details generated by the windows adhere to a globally consistent motion trajectory.

**3. Panoramic Projection and Temporal Extension**
*   **Spherical Consistency:** For VR applications, operating directly on Equirectangular Projections (ERP) causes distortion. We will implement a projection module that maps the spherical latent data into perspective viewports for denoising, then re-projects them back to the sphere. The shifting window logic will apply to these viewports to ensure the spherical reconstruction is seamless.
*   **Temporal Scaling:** We will extend the shifting window concept to the time dimension. by shifting the context window across frames during generation, we can generate videos of arbitrary length. By treating the first and last frames as connected boundaries (similar to the $360^{\circ}$ spatial logic), we can also enforce loopable video generation.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Scalability:** A training-free method to generate video content of arbitrary aspect ratios and resolutions using standard, fixed-resolution models.
*   **Immersive Capability:** The ability to generate seamless $360^{\circ}$ panoramic videos with correct motion physics and no boundary artifacts.
*   **Efficiency:** A solution that decouples output resolution from VRAM usage, allowing for the generation of large-scale scenes on consumer hardware.
*   **Versatility:** Support for infinite-length and loopable video generation, crucial for background assets in virtual environments.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a framework to generate spatially scalable and panoramic dynamic scenes. The following setup details were used to produce the empirical results.

*   **Base Models:** We built our method upon the existing text-to-video generation model **VideoCrafter2** and the image-to-video generation model **VideoCrafterl**.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **360DVD:** Used for direct comparison in dynamic panorama generation.
    *   **4K4DGen:** Compared in feature capabilities and random case user studies.
    *   **Scalecrafter:** Compared in feature capabilities and random case user studies.
    *   **VividDream:** Compared in feature capabilities and random case user studies.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Automated Metrics:** CLIP-Score, Image Quality, Dynamic Degree, Motion Smoothness, Temporal Flickering, Scene Richness.
    *   **Visual-Language Model Scoring:** Q-Align (Image Quality) and Q-Align (Video Quality).
    *   **User Study Criteria:** Graphics Quality, Frame Consistency, End Continuity (Left-Right), Motion Pattern, and Scene Richness.
*   **Evaluation Protocol:**
    *   We assessed visual quality by randomly selecting views from **100 generated video cases** using random camera positions.
    *   Key factors were evaluated according to **VBench** and **CogVideoX** protocols.
*   **User Study Details:**
    *   **Participants:** 20 participants.
    *   **Task:** Select the video with the highest quality based on five specific criteria.
    *   **Comparison Types:** "Same Case Comparison" (same scene) and "Random Case Comparison" (different scenes due to limited sample availability).
    *   **Rating Scale:** 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest).

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1A: Feature Capability Comparison of Dynamic Scene Generation Methods**
| Method | Tuning-Free | Arbitrary Size | 360 Field-of-View | Text Only Condition | Image Condition | Unlimited Video Length | Loopable Generation |

**Table 2: User Preference Study Results (Rating 1-5)**

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

**Table 3: Ablation Study Performance Comparison**
*Note: OOM = Out-of-Memory*

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| w/o GMG | 0.571 | 0.765 | 0.961 | 0.946 | 0.598 |
| **Full Method** | **0.587** | **0.778** | **0.967** | **0.985** | **0.616** |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**General Capabilities**
*   We observed that the framework successfully generated regular panoramas with arbitrary aspect ratios and 360-degree panoramic views.
*   We verified the system supports both text-to-video (T2V) and image-to-video (I2V) conditioning.
*   We generated successful outputs for diverse prompts, including thunderstorms, northern lights, and underwater scenes.

**Component Analysis (Ablation Observations)**
*   **Direct Inference:** We attempted to generate video directly at the target resolution without our enhancement techniques. This resulted in an Out-of-Memory (OOM) error due to high VRAM demands.
*   **Without Offset Shifting Denoising (w/o OSD):** Removing OSD resulted in visible seams and multi-scale artifacts where window boundaries occurred. The content distribution appeared disjointed (e.g., disjointed hot air balloons or cherry blossom branches).
*   **Without Global Motion Guidance (w/o GMG):** Omitting GMG reduced frame-to-frame motion continuity. While local details were generated, the overall motion structure lacked global coherence.
*   **Full Method:** Integrating all components yielded the highest visual fidelity, seamless transitions, and consistent motion.

**Boundary and Temporal Continuity**
*   **Spatial Seamlessness:** By horizontally concatenating generated video frames, we observed that regions near the horizontal boundaries aligned seamlessly, confirming the effectiveness of the method for 360-degree viewing.
*   **Temporal Extension:** We successfully generated long videos (beyond the standard 16 frames of the base model). Examining frames at indices 1, 16, 32, 48, 64, and 80 showed consistent visual quality and smooth transitions (e.g., a sailboat moving naturally through a changing lighting environment).
*   **Looping:** We confirmed the ability to generate loopable video where the end of the sequence transitions smoothly back to the start.

**Methodological Validation**
*   **Offset Shifting:** We observed that shifting denoising windows vertically and horizontally created "overlap" regions between steps. This successfully mitigated artifacts and synchronized the denoising process across the entire panorama.
*   **Panoramic Projection:** Projecting spherical latents into perspective view ports, denoising, and re-projecting reduced distortion compared to standard methods.

Our pipeline is divided into two stages: low-resolution stage establishes a coarse motion structure, 360-degree setting(the yellow block) involves Panoramic Projecting Denoise to initialize motion that fits to spherical panorama, while the regular perspective setting(the blue block) utilizes Offset Shifting with overlap for the early denoise steps, then the remaining denoise steps are completed by our Offset Shifting Denoise. The up-scaling stage(the green block) utilizes more shift windows to produce a refined, high-resolution panorama with Global Motion Guidance from the low-resoltuion video.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 5:
  - Filename: figure_7.png
  - Caption: Figure 7. To demonstrates the seamlessness of generated panorama videos, we horizontally concatenat the video frames, showcasing continuity across the left and right boundaries.
--------------------------------------------------

  - Caption: Figure 8. Qualitative visualization of ablation study in regular perspective setting. Refer to our project page for results in video format.

  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. The purposed Offset Shifting Window mechanism, which involves shifting denoising windows both vertically and horizontally between denoise steps to denoise the whole panorama video latent with arbitrary aspect ratio an resolution. The denosing windows are shifted vertically and horizontally every step, creating ”overlap” regions between steps which mitigate the artifacts and synchronize the whole denoising process across the panorama. This results in seamless and consistent panoramic video generation with high resolution and aspect ratio.
--------------------------------------------------

The purposed Panoramic Projecting Denoise, where spherical panorama videos latents (represented as equirectangular projections) are projected into perspective view port windows and denoised, followed by re-projection back to the equirectangular panorama, as shown in the upper part of the figure. Those view port windows are also shifted with an offset applied in their view angles at each steps, as shown in the lower part of the figure. For legibility, only a proportion of view port regions are shown in the figure.
--------------------------------------------------

prompt.name: SYSTEM.md
prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables
```latex
\begin{table}
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
    \toprule
    Method & Frobnability \\
    \midrule
    Theirs & Frumpy \\
    Yours & Frobbly \\
    Ours & Makes one's heart Frob\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \caption{Results.   Ours is better.}
  \label{tab:example}
\end{table}
```

## Example Code for Figures
```latex
\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{0.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
   %\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{egfigure.eps}

   \caption{Example of caption.
   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}
  \centering
  \begin{subfigure}{0.68\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-a}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill
  \begin{subfigure}{0.28\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The increasing demand for immersive AR/VR applications necessitates the generation of high-quality, scene-level, and $360^\circ$ panoramic videos. However, current state-of-the-art video diffusion models are fundamentally constrained by fixed training resolutions and aspect ratios (typically square or standard landscape). Extending these models to synthesize panoramic dynamic content presents three critical technical barriers:

1.  **Resolution and Aspect Ratio Constraints:** Generating ultra-wide or high-resolution content requires computational resources that scale quadratically, often exceeding GPU memory limits. Existing patch-stitching methods used for static images fail to maintain global motion coherence when applied to video, resulting in fragmented dynamics.
2.  **Geometric Distortion in $360^\circ$ Fields:** Equirectangular projections (ERP) introduce severe polar distortion and require seamless continuity at the left-right meridian. Standard diffusion models trained on perspective imagery cannot natively handle these geometric properties, leading to seams and warped content.
3.  **Temporal Scalability:** Current models operate on fixed frame lengths (e.g., 16 frames). Generating long-duration or loopable panoramic videos requires ensuring temporal consistency beyond the model's fixed context window, which remains an unsolved challenge for high-resolution wide-field inputs.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **DynamicScaler**, a unified, training-free framework designed to enable spatially scalable and panoramic dynamic scene synthesis using pre-trained video diffusion models.

Our core hypothesis is that we can achieve seamless spatial and temporal coherence across arbitrary resolutions without fine-tuning by introducing a **Offset Shifting Denoiser (OSD)**. We posit that by shifting the receptive field (denoising window) by a calculated offset at each diffusion timestep, we can implicitly synchronize the noise distribution across the entire panoramic latent space. This "rotating window" approach will distribute global context and erase boundary artifacts. Furthermore, we hypothesize that a **Global Motion Guidance (GMG)** mechanism—utilizing a low-resolution motion prior—will ensure that local windowed generation adheres to a consistent global motion trajectory.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a pipeline capable of generating regular panoramas with arbitrary aspect ratios and full $360^\circ$ views. The architecture consists of the Offset Shifting Denoiser, Global Motion Guidance, and a Panoramic Projection mechanism.

### 1. Offset Shifting Denoising (OSD)
To generate a panorama latent $Z$ of size $W_p \times H_p$ using a base model $\theta$ trained on a smaller resolution $W_\theta \times H_\theta$, we will employ a window-based approach. Unlike standard multi-diffusion which requires computationally expensive explicit overlaps, we will implement a shifting strategy.

At each denoising step $t$, the panoramic latent $Z$ will be divided into $n_W \times n_H$ windows. We will apply a spatial offset to these windows, shifting them both vertically and horizontally. This creates "implicit overlap" regions between steps, synchronizing content across the global latent.
*   **Vertical Handling:** Windows shift vertically; residual top/bottom regions are handled by padding windows.
*   **Horizontal Handling (Ring Buffer):** For panoramic continuity, the left and right boundaries will be treated as connected. Windows crossing the right boundary will wrap to the left.

We formulate the update rule for the panoramic latent $Z_t$ as:

$$ Z_{t} = Con|_{1:n_{W}, 1:n_{H}} (\Phi_{\theta}(t, c, Split(Z_{t-1}, i, j, t, n_{W}, n_{H}))) $$

Where:
*   $\Phi_{\theta}$ represents the diffusion denoising process.
*   $Split(X, i, j, t, n_W, n_H)$ divides the latent $X$ into windows with a time-dependent offset at time $t$, selecting the window in the $i$-th column and $j$-th row.
*   $Con(\cdot)$ collects latents from divided windows and concatenates them to reconstruct the full panorama.
*   $c$ represents the conditioning (text or image).

### 2. Global Motion Guidance (GMG)
To prevent motion divergence in high-resolution scenes (e.g., a waterfall flowing inconsistently across windows), we will implement a hierarchical generation process.

1.  **Low-Resolution Stage:** We first synthesize a video at a lower resolution ($Z_{LRT}$) to establish the coarse motion structure.
2.  **Upscaling and Guidance:** We upsample this result using interpolation $inter(\cdot)$ and add noise $noise(\cdot)$ to serve as the initialization for the high-resolution generation.

The formulation for the initialization of the high-resolution latent $Z_{HR^0}$ is:

$$ Z_{HR^{0}} = \Phi_{\theta}^{OSD}(noise(inter(\Phi_{\theta}^{OSD}(Z_{LRT})))) $$

This ensures that the subsequent high-resolution OSD process refines local details while adhering to the global motion layout established in the first stage.

### 3. $360^\circ$ FoV Panorama Generation
To handle the specific geometry of $360^\circ$ videos, we will map the spherical panorama to Equirectangular Projection (ERP). Since standard models assume perspective projection, we will implement a **Panoramic Projection Denoiser**.

#### Spherical Projection Mapping
We define the mapping from a point $(x, y, z)$ on the unit sphere to longitude $\alpha$ and latitude $\beta$:
$$ \alpha = \arctan2(y, x), \quad \beta = \arcsin(z) $$
The ERP maps $(\alpha, \beta)$ to a rectangular plane $(u, v)$ where $u=\alpha$ and $v=\beta$.

#### Projection-Based Denoising
Instead of denoising the ERP image directly (which causes distortion), we will project portions of the ERP latent $Z^p$ into perspective viewports using a projection function $Proj(\cdot)$. We will shift these viewports by an angular offset $a$ at each timestep to ensure coverage.

$$ Z_{t} = Con_{Proj}|_{1:n_{\alpha}, 1:n_{\beta}} (\Phi_{\theta}(t, c, Proj(Z_{t-1}, f, a_{i,j,t}))) $$

Where $Con_{Proj}$ projects the denoised perspective latents back onto the $360^\circ$ ERP sphere.

#### Noise Rebalancing
To address inconsistent noise levels in regions where viewports overlap, we will maintain a mask $M_d$ tracking denoised regions. We will rebalance the noise before the diffusion step:

$$ Z_{t}^{\prime}[x, y] = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \sqrt{\alpha_{t}} Z_{t}[x, y] + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_{t}} \epsilon_{t} & \mathrm{if} \ M_{d}(x, y) = 1 \\ Z_{t}[x, y] & \mathrm{if} \ M_{d}(x, y) = 0 \end{array} \right. $$

This ensures uniform noise distribution entering the model $\theta$.

### 4. Temporal Scalability (Long and Loopable Video)
We will extend the OSD mechanism to the temporal dimension to generate videos exceeding the model's frame limit $F_\theta$.

The target latent $\bar{Z}$ of length $F'$ will be divided into $n_F$ clips. We will apply a temporal offset shift at each timestep:

$$ Z_{t} = Con_{F}|_{1:n_{F}} (\Phi_{\theta}(t, c, Split_{F}(Z_{t-1}, i, t, n_{F}))) $$

To achieve **loopable generation**, we will treat the temporal dimension as a ring buffer (similar to the spatial horizontal boundary), allowing windows to cross from the last frame back to the first frame, ensuring the start and end of the video are seamless.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to deliver the following theoretical and practical contributions to the field of generative computer vision:

1.  **Unified Scalability Framework:** A single, tuning-free architecture that solves resolution, aspect ratio, and temporal duration constraints simultaneously using standard pre-trained video diffusion models.
2.  **Constant VRAM Consumption:** By processing via shifting windows, we expect the memory footprint to remain constant regardless of the output video resolution, enabling the generation of massive panoramas on consumer hardware.
3.  **Geometric Consistency:** The Panoramic Projection Denoiser will theoretically eliminate the polar distortion and seam artifacts common in latent-based 360 generation.
4.  **Global Motion Coherence:** The proposed GMG mechanism is expected to solve the disjointed motion artifacts typical of patch-based generation, enabling complex, scene-wide dynamics (e.g., flowing rivers, moving clouds) to remain consistent across arbitrary fields of view.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

tools.permissions: upstream's own agent settings; provider web search denied by managed settings (Claude Code permissions.deny WebSearch, Codex web_search="disabled")

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
